description: Replica Netflix account-cancellation page (the user has clicked Cancel Membership and is on the retention/confirmation step). Deliberately injected dark patterns and counterexamples. Used to measure the identification prompt's true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative rates on a Streaming & entertainment fixture where the dominant DP signature is RETENTION friction.
page_url_when_served: http://localhost:8000/fixtures/netflix-cancel-flow/netflix-cancel-flow.html (or any http:// host; the extension rejects file:// URLs)

expected_page_evaluation.scoring_note: Mark page_evaluation correct if page_type ∈ {cancellation, settings, account_management} AND user_primary_intent is a reasonable paraphrase of 'cancel my Netflix membership'. Vague intents ('manage my account', 'browse Netflix') or wrong ones ('subscribe', 'pause') are incorrect — the user came to cancel, the page is trying to talk them out of it. Every downstream harm test depends on this being correctly identified as a cancellation flow with cancel intent (not a retention/upsell flow with subscribe intent).

dark_patterns.element: Pre-selected 'Pause your membership' radio (the costliest-to-the-user retention option) with a 'Most Popular' pill tag, marked as the highlighted card
dark_patterns.why: The user came to CANCEL. The Pause option is pre-selected (radio checked, card highlighted with red border + tinted background + 'Most Popular' pill), reversing the user's revealed intent. Pre-selecting a paid-retention outcome (continued billing after the 3-month pause expires at the same US$22.99/month) inside a cancel flow benefits Netflix (recovered revenue) at the user's cost. Famous Netflix retention pattern.

dark_patterns.element: Giant red 'PAUSE MY MEMBERSHIP' pill button (full-width, 17px bold uppercase) — vs the cancel-completion link below it (DP-3) which is 11px gray no-underline
dark_patterns.why: The user came to cancel. The visually dominant action is the PAUSE pill (full-width, bright Netflix red, 17px bold, uppercase, prominent border-radius), while the option that matches the user's revealed intent (cancel — see DP-3's link, which is 11px gray, no-underline, lowercase, light font-weight) is visually buried directly below it. Prominence misaligned with revealed user intent — not a feature suggestion, a deliberate visual demotion. Distinct from CE-2 (the 'End my membership now' button, which is also visible but secondary).

dark_patterns.element: Tiny gray cancellation link below the pause pill: 'Yes, cancel anyway and lose my watchlist, recommendations, continue-watching progress, and downloaded titles'
dark_patterns.why: The cancel-completion link's LABEL frames the user's choice as a self-inflicted loss enumerated in concrete terms (watchlist, recommendations, continue-watching, downloaded titles). The user can cancel (the link is functional), but the decline option itself shames the user for declining by listing every personalization artifact they will lose. Manipulation is in the wording of the action control, not the action it performs. Canonical Netflix shame language. NOTE: this same element is also the visually-buried half of the False hierarchy pair with DP-2 (the PAUSE pill) — a model that flags this link with type=False hierarchy is making a defensible call grounded in the same harm test, hence the dual accepts_types.

counterexamples.element: 'Sign out' link in the top nav header
counterexamples.why_not: A standard navigation link present on every Netflix account page. Nothing on this cancellation page depends on the user signing out, and the link doesn't gate or coerce. Account-management nav affordances are routine.

counterexamples.element: The 'End my membership now' button — full-width, dark-bordered, secondary visual prominence below the pause pill
counterexamples.why_not: This IS the legitimate cancel CTA — it does what its label promises (navigates to the cancel-confirmation page). Visually less prominent than the pause pill (DP-2) but NOT visually buried: full-width, clearly bordered, easily clickable, label exactly matches the action. The harm test for False hierarchy requires the legitimate option be visually buried against user intent (e.g., 11px gray no-underline link); this button doesn't meet that test. The actually-buried cancel option is DP-3 (the confirm-shaming link) — the model should distinguish them. Compare DP-2 (the pause pill) which IS the visually-dominant misaligned-with-intent CTA.

counterexamples.element: 'Your current plan' summary card listing plan tier, monthly cost, next billing date, member-since date
counterexamples.why_not: All decision-critical billing info is visible up front — plan tier, US$22.99/month, June 14 billing date, member-since date. Nothing is collapsed, hidden, or buried. This is a normal account-state-summary surface.

counterexamples.element: Pre-checked 'Email me a confirmation receipt of this change' checkbox
counterexamples.why_not: A pre-checked checkbox inside a settings flow — visually adjacent to DP-1 (the pre-selected pause radio) — but the option is a sensible transactional default: sending the user a record of an account-state change they just made. Not a paid add-on, not marketing, not data extraction. Users overwhelmingly want a written confirmation of a cancellation. Compare DP-1 (paid retention pre-selected) — same surface shape (a default checkmark), opposite harm-test answer.

counterexamples.element: 'Need a hand? Visit our Help Center or call …' link in the page footer
counterexamples.why_not: A footer help link is not coercive friction — it's an optional support affordance that the user can ignore entirely while completing cancellation. The harm test for Forced Action requires the user be FORCED to take an action; this link doesn't force anything. Compare a hypothetical 'You must visit Help Center before cancelling' gate which WOULD be Forced Action.

fixture_notes: 3 DPs after the 2026-05 realism audit (issue #27). Originally 8 DPs; dropped 5 as not canonical for Netflix cancel: dp-disguised-partner-ad (Netflix has no Spotify integration and does not show partner cross-promos on cancel), dp-fake-retention-stats (Netflix retains via 'lose your watchlist' framing, not via retention statistics), dp-trick-wording-confirm (Netflix does not use double-negative buttons on cancel), dp-hidden-cancel-terms (Netflix actually SURFACES post-cancel consequences as part of the shame copy — they are not hidden), dp-popup-games (Netflix does not pop a Games modal on cancel).

The remaining 3 DPs are all canonical Netflix retention patterns: Pause-as-default (DP-1 — famous), PAUSE pill vs cancel-link visual hierarchy (DP-2), and the watchlist-loss enumeration in the cancel link wording (DP-3).
Disguised ad, Trick wording, Pop-up ad, Hidden information, Fake social proof, and Forced Action have no coverage on this fixture by design — see issue #27 for the cross-fixture rationale.

scoring.true_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `dark_patterns` gt_id (by selector / html_evidence overlap) AND whose dark_pattern_type is in that entry's `accepts_types`.
scoring.false_negative: A `dark_patterns` gt_id has no matching entry in the model output.
scoring.false_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `counterexamples` gt_id, OR an entry whose target element matches no gt_id at all.
scoring.wrong_type: Model flags the right element (a `dark_patterns` gt_id) but with a dark_pattern_type NOT in `accepts_types`. Count separately from TP/FP — found something real but mislabeled it.
scoring.page_eval: Separately, score expected_page_evaluation as correct/incorrect per its scoring_note.
headline_metrics: recall = TP / (TP + FN)   [TP + FN = 3, the count of injected dark patterns post-audit]
false_positive_rate = FP / (number of counterexamples + extraneous flags) — this is the metric the recent prompt rewrite targets
Note: maxItems is 3 in the schema, so the model can report at most 3 patterns per run. Recall is no longer bounded by the schema cap on this fixture.
